doc.title: Jon Weber interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, June 2, 2012

title: Learning ranges from players; the game of what do you give them
summary: He learned voicing and ranges by asking players, then introduces the game of what to play for a famous person who walks in.

story.theme_name: Writing and arranging: how musicians compose
story.community_name: Writing, arranging and composing: how the music gets made

blocks.x: So you just learned about voicing and ranges and all that from listening and talking to the players?

Yes. Trial and error and I’d ask them, I’d say “what’s the highest note you want to hit on a tenor saxophone?” “Well you get to this point and then you hit an altissimo.” “All right, what’s the best range for a trombone? What’s the toughest position?” “Seventh. Stay away from it.” And then Henry Mancini of all people — I was playing a gig in a hotel, quite young, and he walks in. What do you give him? I have a game with my best friend, John Ramirez back in Chicago, we call “what do you give ‘em?” Which means if somebody famous comes in, what do you have ready for them that’s going to blow them away. We also have a game called “what don’t you give?” For example, if Francis Ford Coppola walks in, do not give him Godfather I, Godfather II. Don’t do that. But for

example, if Paul McCartney were to walk in what do you give him? Well I’m not going to give him a Beatle song, I’m not going to even give him a post-Beatle song. I’m going to lay this one on him. Do I have time to give this 30-second anecdote?
